title: Combatting Online Harms Through Innovation: A Report to Congress

evidence.quote: human intervention is still needed, and perhaps always will be, in connection with monitoring the use and decisions of AI tools intended to address harmful content

Simply placing moderators, trust and safety professionals, and other people in AI oversight roles is insufficient. The work is challenging and demands that moderators have adequate training, time, agency to make decisions, and workplace protections.

AI use in this area needs to be meaningfully transparent, which includes the need for it to be explainable and contestable, especially when people's rights are involved or when personal data is being collected or used.
companies should ensure that users know when automated tools are making moderation decisions and should have 'a high level understanding' of the decision-making logic
accountability would include meaningful appeal and redress mechanisms for consumers and others...and the use of independent audits and algorithmic impact assessments (AIAs)

to ensure that the tools are reliable and effective, companies should pursue and monitor detection methods for accuracy and nondiscrimination, submit to regular assessments, and be 'encouraged to publicly share data about the accuracy of their systems and to open their process and algorithmic systems to periodic external auditing'
Algorithmic Impact Assessments (AIAs) are a means of assessing AI systems in the private or public sector...They allow for the evaluation of an AI system's impact before, during, or after its use.
data scientists and their employers who build AI tools — as well as the firms procuring and deploying them — are responsible for both inputs and outputs
One important and practical consideration is having adequate documentation throughout the AI development process.
Appropriate documentation of the datasets, models, and work undertaken to create these tools is important in this regard.

A major collaborative effort to advance authentication tools is the Coalition for Content Provenance for Authenticity (C2PA)...The goal of this coalition is to create an 'open technical standard providing publishers, creators, and consumers the ability to trace the origin of different types of media.'
Congress should generally steer clear of laws that require, assume the use of, or pressure companies to deploy AI tools to detect harmful content
we believe any initial legislative focus should prioritize the transparency and accountability of platforms and others that build and use automated systems to address online harms
calls for: (1) public disclosure of information, including policies and data on the use and impact of AI systems; (2) researcher access to additional information
it seems clear that only legislation will allow us to crack open the black boxes of content moderation

policy_extraction.implementation_notes: This is a report to Congress mandated by the 2021 Appropriations Act (American COMPETE Act). It is analytical and advisory in nature, not binding regulation. The FTC recommends against mandating AI use for content moderation and instead calls for transparency, accountability, and human oversight frameworks. The report covers a broad range of online harms (deepfakes, CSAM, fraud, TVEC, disinformation, harassment) but explicitly defers on terrorism, election security, and criminal matters to other agencies (DHS, DOJ, State Department). The report recommends legislation focused on platform transparency and algorithmic accountability rather than prescriptive AI deployment mandates. No civil or criminal penalties are specified; enforcement is envisioned through future legislation. Confidence is high for jurisdiction and issuing body, but moderate for safety requirement labels as many are framed as recommendations rather than current requirements.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The document is primarily framed around consumer and public safety: the FTC's congressional mandate centers on whether AI can identify and address specified harms to individuals online—scams, deepfakes, CSAM, harassment, illegal drug sales, etc. The report consistently evaluates AI tools through the lens of consumer protection, harm reduction, and public safety outcomes. Secondary framing includes fundamental rights (bias, discrimination, censorship, First Amendment concerns, appeal rights) and social stability (disinformation, hate crimes, violent extremism, election integrity).

evidence_spans.quote: Congress directed the Federal Trade Commission to study and report on whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) 'may be used to identify, remove, or take any other appropriate action necessary to address' a wide variety of specified 'online harms.'

The key conclusion of this report is thus that governments, platforms, and others must exercise great caution in either mandating the use of, or over-relying on, these tools even for the important purpose of reducing harms.

these tools remain largely rudimentary, have substantial limitations, and may never be appropriate in some cases as an alternative to human judgment. Their use — both now and in the future — raises a host of persistent legal and policy concerns.

The use of AI in the automated detection of online harms is certainly not immune to these issues. For example, large language models used to moderate online content can result in biased and discriminatory results

When the use of an AI detection tool results in false positives, or overblocking, it may serve to reduce freedom of expression. This problem is especially acute when those silenced are members of historically marginalized communities.
